common_name: Firewitch Dianthus (Perennial Plant of the Year Magenta Cheddar Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; cheddar pinks cultivars are among the most drought- and heat-tolerant perennials available, thriving in lean, rocky, or sandy soils where richer soil causes rot.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Firewitch was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 2006, prized for its dense, low mat of needle-like, silvery-blue evergreen foliage that stays attractive year-round, covered in spring by an abundance of fragrant, clove-scented, vivid magenta-pink flowers. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, rocky, or sandy soil where richer, moister conditions actually shorten its life, making it an excellent choice for a rock garden, dry border edge, or the gaps between paving stones. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat tidy and encourage denser growth, and avoid heavy mulch or rich soil that can cause crown rot.

common_name: Bath's Pink Dianthus (Heat-Tolerant Southern Groundcover Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; cheddar pinks cultivars are among the most drought- and heat-tolerant perennials available, thriving in lean, rocky, or sandy soils where richer soil causes rot.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Bath's Pink was discovered and named by a Georgia gardener and has become one of the most reliable cheddar pink selections for hot, humid Southern gardens, forming a dense, low mat of fine, silvery-blue foliage topped in spring with abundant fragrant, soft pink, fringed flowers. It shows notably better heat and humidity tolerance than many other dianthus cultivars, an important quality for gardeners south of the plant's more typical cooler range, and it thrives in the same lean, sharply drained, rocky-to-sandy soil that other cheddar pinks require. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

common_name: Snow Lady Shasta Daisy (Compact Dwarf White Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Snow Lady is an AAS-winning dwarf shasta daisy that blooms the first year from an early seed start and stays much more compact than the tall classic shasta daisy.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Snow Lady is a compact, All-America Selections-winning shasta daisy cultivar producing classic, crisp white, yellow-centered daisy flowers on a dwarf plant well under a foot tall, much shorter than the standard shasta daisy, making it a good fit for the front of a border, edging, or containers where taller cultivars would be out of scale. It flowers reliably the first year from an early seed start and continues blooming over a long summer season with regular deadheading. It is easy to grow in average garden soil and, like other shasta daisies, benefits from division every two to three years to maintain vigor as clumps become congested.

common_name: Sunkiss Coreopsis (AAS-Winning Bicolor Red-Ringed Yellow Coreopsis)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sunkiss is an AAS-winning bicolor coreopsis blooming heavily the first year from an early start.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Sunkiss is an All-America Selections-winning coreopsis producing bright golden-yellow flowers marked with a bold burgundy-red ring around the center, a striking bicolor pattern that stands out against the plain gold of most coreopsis cultivars. It blooms heavily from its first year onward and continues over a long summer season with regular deadheading, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil with ease once established. Like other coreopsis, it performs best in lean soil with sharp drainage, since overly rich or wet conditions promote excess foliage and shorten the plant's life; dividing congested clumps every few years helps maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Route 66 produces striking golden-yellow flowers with a bold burgundy-red central splash that intensifies as the bloom ages, giving each flower a distinctive pinwheel-like pattern.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Route 66 is a bold bicolor coreopsis cultivar producing bright yellow flowers marked with a distinctive burgundy-red central splash that spreads and intensifies as each bloom matures, giving individual flowers on the same plant a range of patterning from mostly yellow to nearly half red. It blooms over a long summer season and, like other coreopsis, tolerates heat, drought, and lean soil with ease once established, making it a low-maintenance choice for a sunny border or mass planting. Deadheading spent flowers encourages continued bloom, and dividing congested clumps every few years in spring helps maintain the plant's vigor.
